claim: The C2A domain of UNC-13L displays two conserved binding modes: forming C2A/C2A homodimers, or forming a heterodimer with the zinc finger domain of UNC-10/RIM (C2A/RIM).
source: Here we show that the C2A domain of UNC-13L, like the corresponding domain in mammalian Munc13-1, displays two conserved binding modes: forming C2A/C2A homodimers, or forming a heterodimer with the zinc finger domain of UNC-10/RIM (C2A/RIM).
evidence: Supported by gel filtration analysis (Figure 1C), ITC experiments (Figure 1E,F), and co-immunoprecipitation (Figure 1D) showing homodimer and heterodimer formation.

claim: UNC-13L's C2A promotes synaptic transmission by regulating a post-priming process.
source: Functional analysis revealed that UNC-13L's C2A promotes synaptic transmission by regulating a post-priming process.
evidence: Based on functional analysis showing effects on release but not priming, as detailed in the results section.

claim: Stimulus-evoked release but not SV priming was impaired in unc-10 mutants deficient for C2A/RIM heterodimerization.
source: Stimulus-evoked release but not SV priming, was impaired in unc-10 mutants deficient for C2A/RIM heterodimerization, leading to decreased release probability.
evidence: Demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings showing reduced evoked EPSCs but normal sucrose-evoked responses in unc-10(nu487 K77/79E) mutants (Figure 3).

claim: Disrupting C2A/C2A homodimerization in UNC-13L-rescued animals had no effect on synaptic transmission.
source: Disrupting C2A/C2A homodimerization in UNC-13L-rescued animals had no effect on synaptic transmission, but fully restored the evoked release and the release probability of unc-10/RIM mutants deficient for C2A/RIM heterodimerization.
evidence: Shown by normal mEPSCs and evoked EPSCs in UNC-13L(K49E) rescue animals (Figures 2 and 3).

claim: RIM binding C2A releases UNC-13L from an autoinhibitory homodimeric complex to become fusion-competent by functioning as a switch only.
source: Thus, our results support the model that RIM binding C2A releases UNC-13L from an autoinhibitory homodimeric complex to become fusion-competent by functioning as a switch only.
evidence: Inferred from the rescue of synaptic transmission defects in double mutants blocking both homo- and heterodimerization.

claim: The UNC-13L C2A domain and the UNC-10/RIM ZF domain share high sequence identity with the corresponding domains of mouse Munc13-1 (50%) and RIM (48%).
source: The UNC-13L C2A domain and the UNC-10/RIM ZF domain share high sequence identity with the corresponding domains of mouse Munc13-1 (50%) and RIM (48%) (Figure 1A,B)
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: Recombinant C2A forms a homodimer, and this homodimerization was disrupted by a K49E mutation.
source: Gel filtration analysis indicated that recombinant C2A forms a homodimer, and that this homodimerization was disrupted by a mutation (K49E) analogous to that which disrupts Munc13-1 homodimerization (Figure 1A,C) (Lu et al., 2006; Deng et al., 2011).
evidence: Demonstrated by gel filtration showing different elution volumes for wild-type and K49E mutant C2A (Figure 1C).

claim: The UNC-13L C2A domain tightly binds the UNC-10/RIM ZF domain with a Kd of 1.29 µM.
source: Our results showed that the UNC-13L C2A domain tightly binds the UNC-10/RIM ZF domain (Kd = 1.29 µM, Figure 1D,E)
evidence: Measured by isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) experiments (Figure 1E).

claim: The interaction between UNC-13L C2A and UNC-10/RIM ZF was eliminated by a K77/79E double mutation in the ZF domain.
source: and that this interaction was eliminated by a double mutation in the ZF domain (K77/79E), which is analogous to mutations that disrupt binding of the corresponding mammalian Munc13-1 and RIM domains (Figure 1D–F) (Dulubova et al., 2005).
evidence: Shown by co-immunoprecipitation (Figure 1D) and ITC (Figure 1F) experiments.

claim: Deleting the C2A domain (UNC-13LΔC2A) significantly decreased mEPSC frequency in both 0 mM and 1 mM Ca2+.
source: Deleting the C2A domain (UNC-13LΔC2A) significantly decreased mEPSC frequency in both 0 mM and 1 mM Ca2+ (Figure 2B,E, Table 1), demonstrating an important role of the C2A domain in tonic acetylcholine (ACh) release.
evidence: Demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings of mEPSCs (Figure 2B,E, Table 1).

claim: The mIPSC frequency was significantly decreased in the UNC-13LΔC2A rescue animals in 0 mM Ca2+ but was unchanged in 1 mM Ca2+.
source: The mIPSC frequency was significantly decreased in the UNC-13LΔC2A rescue animals in 0 mM Ca2+ (Figure 2C, Table 1), but was unchanged in 1 mM Ca2+, compared to that in the UNC-13L rescue animals (Figure 2F).
evidence: Shown by mIPSC recordings at different calcium concentrations (Figure 2C,F, Table 1).

claim: The mEPSC and mIPSC frequencies in the UNC-13L(K49E) rescue animals were comparable to those in the UNC-13L rescue animals in both 0 mM and 1 mM Ca2+.
source: The mEPSC and mIPSC frequencies in the UNC-13L(K49E) rescue animals were comparable to those in the UNC-13L rescue animals in both 0 mM and 1 mM Ca2+ conditions (Figure 2A–F, Table 1), indicating that homodimerization does not affect tonic ACh or GABA release.
evidence: Demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings (Figure 2A-F, Table 1).

claim: The mEPSCs and mIPSCs were markedly reduced in unc-10(nu487 K77/79E) mutants in 0 mM Ca2+, whereas both were unaltered in 1 mM Ca2+.
source: Analysis of tonic release showed that the mEPSCs and mIPSCs were markedly reduced in unc-10(nu487 K77/79E) mutants in 0 mM Ca2+, whereas both were unaltered in 1 mM Ca2+ (Figure 2A–F)
evidence: Shown by electrophysiological recordings at different calcium concentrations (Figure 2A-F).

claim: C2A/RIM heterodimerization is only required for tonic release in low Ca2+ when release probability is reduced.
source: suggesting that C2A/RIM heterodimerization is only required for tonic release in low Ca2+ when release probability is reduced.
evidence: Inferred from the calcium-dependent effects on mEPSCs and mIPSCs in unc-10(nu487 K77/79E) mutants (Figure 2).

claim: The UNC-13L(K49E); unc-10(nu487 K77/79E) double mutant mIPSC rate in 0 mM Ca2+ was significantly higher than that observed in unc-10(nu487 K77/79E) single mutants.
source: In 0 mM Ca2+ recordings, the UNC-13L(K49E); unc-10(nu487 K77/79E) double mutant mIPSC rate was significantly higher than that observed in unc-10(nu487 K77/79E) single mutants, suggesting that blocking homodimer formation was sufficient to prevent the decreased tonic GABA release caused by the unc-10(nu487 K77/79E) mutation (Figure 2C).
evidence: Demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings (Figure 2C).

claim: Blocking homodimerization did not significantly improve mEPSC rates in 0 mM Ca2+ in unc-10(nu487 K77/79E) mutants.
source: By contrast, blocking homodimerization did not significantly improve mEPSC rates in 0 mM Ca2+ in unc-10(nu487 K77/79E) mutants (Figure 2B).
evidence: Shown by electrophysiological recordings (Figure 2B).

claim: Heterodimerization increases tonic GABA release by preventing homodimer formation, whereas heterodimerization promotes tonic ACh release by a distinct mechanism.
source: Thus, heterodimerization increases tonic GABA release by preventing homodimer formation, whereas heterodimerization promotes tonic ACh release by a distinct mechanism.
evidence: Inferred from differential effects of blocking homodimerization on mEPSCs versus mIPSCs in unc-10 mutants.

claim: UNC-13LΔC2A exhibited a smaller evoked EPSC compared to UNC-13L.
source: Compared to UNC-13L, UNC-13LΔC2A exhibited a smaller evoked EPSC (Figure 3A, Table 1), consistent with previous findings (Hu et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2013a).
evidence: Demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings (Figure 3A, Table 1) and supported by previous studies.

claim: The evoked EPSCs were significantly smaller in unc-10(nu487 K77/79E) mutants, exhibiting decreased amplitude and total charge transfer compared to wild-type animals.
source: The evoked EPSCs were significantly smaller in unc-10(nu487 K77/79E) mutants, exhibiting decreased amplitude and total charge transfer compared to wild-type animals (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: Shown by electrophysiological recordings (Figure 3A-C).

claim: The percentage decrease of the evoked charge transfer in the unc-10(nu487 K77/79E) mutant (44%) was similar to that observed in the UNC-13LΔC2A rescue animals (46%).
source: The percentage decrease of the evoked charge transfer in the unc-10(nu487 K77/79E) mutant (44%) was similar to that observed in the UNC-13LΔC2A rescue animals (46%), suggesting that C2A/RIM heterodimerization accounts for the role of the C2A domain in evoked release.
evidence: Calculated from electrophysiological data comparing different genotypes.

claim: C2A/RIM heterodimerization is required for evoked neurotransmitter release.
source: Thus, our results revealed that C2A/RIM heterodimerization is required for evoked neurotransmitter release.
evidence: Inferred from the reduced evoked EPSCs in unc-10(nu487 K77/79E) mutants.

claim: The evoked EPSCs mediated by UNC-13L(K49E) were indistinguishable from those rescued by wild-type UNC-13L.
source: The evoked EPSCs mediated by UNC-13L(K49E) were indistinguishable from those rescued by wild-type UNC-13L, indicating that C2A homodimers are not required for evoked responses (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: Demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings (Figure 3A-C).

claim: Preventing C2A/C2A homodimerization in the unc-10(nu487 K77/79E) mutant fully restored the evoked EPSC to a wild-type level.
source: We found that preventing C2A/C2A homodimerization in the unc-10(nu487 K77/79E) mutant fully restored the evoked EPSC to a wild-type level (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: Shown by electrophysiological recordings in double mutants (Figure 3A-C).

claim: The reduced evoked EPSC caused by blocking C2A/RIM heterodimerization is mediated by increased formation of C2A homodimers.
source: These results suggest that the reduced evoked EPSC caused by blocking C2A/RIM heterodimerization is mediated by increased formation of C2A homodimers.
evidence: Inferred from the rescue of evoked EPSCs in double mutants blocking both interactions.

claim: Munc13-1 homodimers inhibit SV release.
source: These results are consistent with prior analysis of mouse synapses, which suggest that Munc13-1 homodimers inhibit SV release (Deng et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work in mouse synapses.

claim: The monomeric C2A domain is sufficient to support evoked release.
source: These results also demonstrate that the monomeric C2A domain is sufficient to support evoked release, consistent with the observation of tonic release (Figure 2, Table 1).
evidence: Inferred from normal synaptic transmission in double mutants and supported by data in Figure 2 and Table 1.

claim: The RIM ZF domain appears to function only as a switch that releases the C2A domain from the inhibitory homomeric complex.
source: Thus, the RIM ZF domain appears to function only as a switch that releases the C2A domain from the inhibitory homomeric complex.
evidence: Inferred from the complete rescue of synaptic defects by blocking homodimerization in RIM mutants.

claim: UNC-13L lacking the C2A domain could restore the sucrose-evoked current to a wild-type level.
source: Strikingly, UNC-13L lacking the C2A domain could still restore the sucrose-evoked current to a wild-type level (Figure 3E,F, Table 1), indicating that the C2A domain is not required for SV priming.
evidence: Demonstrated by sucrose-evoked current recordings (Figure 3E,F, Table 1).

claim: The C2A domain is not required for SV priming.
source: indicating that the C2A domain is not required for SV priming.
evidence: Inferred from normal sucrose-evoked currents in UNC-13LΔC2A rescue animals.

claim: The sucrose-evoked currents in UNC-13L(K49E) rescue animals and the unc-10(K77/79E) mutant were comparable to those observed in UNC-13L rescue and wild-type animals.
source: Our data showed that the sucrose-evoked currents in these animals were comparable to those observed in UNC-13L rescue and wild-type animals (Figure 3E,F), demonstrating that homodimerization or heterodimerization is not playing a role in SV priming.
evidence: Shown by sucrose-evoked current recordings (Figure 3E,F).

claim: Homodimerization or heterodimerization is not playing a role in SV priming.
source: demonstrating that homodimerization or heterodimerization is not playing a role in SV priming.
evidence: Inferred from normal sucrose-evoked currents in mutants disrupting these interactions.

claim: The probability of synaptic vesicle release (Pvr) was significantly reduced in the ΔC2A rescue and the unc-10(K77/79E) mutant.
source: Consequently, the probability of synaptic vesicle release (Pvr) calculated by the ratio of the charge transfer of the evoked EPSCs to the charge transfer of the sucrose-evoked currents was significantly reduced in the ΔC2A rescue and the unc-10(K77/79E) mutant (Figure 3G).
evidence: Calculated from electrophysiological data (Figure 3G).

claim: The UNC-13L C2A domain regulates release probability by interacting with the UNC-10/RIM, rather than by regulating SV priming.
source: Together, our results demonstrate that the UNC-13L C2A domain regulates release probability by interacting with the UNC-10/RIM, rather than by regulating SV priming.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of normal priming but reduced release probability in relevant mutants.

claim: There were no significant differences in UNC-13 protein expression levels between different rescue lines.
source: By quantifying the mApple fluorescence intensity from different rescue lines, we showed that there were no significant differences (Figure 4A,B), indicating that the UNC-13 proteins were expressed at similar levels in these lines.
evidence: Demonstrated by fluorescence intensity measurements (Figure 4A,B).

claim: The decreased tonic and evoked release in UNC-13LΔC2A rescued animals are unlikely to result from reduced UNC-13L abundance.
source: These results suggest that the decreased tonic and evoked release in UNC-13LΔC2A rescued animals are unlikely to result from reduced UNC-13L abundance.
evidence: Inferred from similar expression levels across different rescue lines.

claim: The C2A domain is crucial for synaptic localization of UNC-13.
source: Prior studies have shown that the C2A domain is crucial for synaptic localization of UNC-13 (Melom et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The decrease in release probability in the UNC-13LΔC2A rescue animals was likely caused by mis-localization of UNC-13 at the active zone.
source: Therefore, it is likely that the decrease in release probability in the UNC-13LΔC2A rescue animals was caused by mis-localization of UNC-13 at the active zone.
evidence: Inferred from prior knowledge about C2A's role in localization and the observed phenotypes.

claim: UNC-13L and ELKS-1 were strongly colocalized in wild-type.
source: UNC-13L and ELKS-1 were strongly colocalized in wild-type (Figure 4C,D)
evidence: Shown by confocal imaging (Figure 4C,D).

claim: The colocalization of UNC-13L and ELKS-1 was not obviously altered in unc-10(K77/79E) mutants.
source: and this colocalization was not obviously altered in unc-10(K77/79E) mutants (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: Shown by confocal imaging (Figure 4E,F).

claim: Disrupting UNC-13L binding to RIM does not prevent synaptic localization of UNC-13L.
source: These results suggest that disrupting UNC-13L binding to RIM does not prevent synaptic localization of UNC-13L.
evidence: Inferred from normal colocalization of UNC-13L with ELKS-1 in unc-10(K77/79E) mutants.

claim: Both the control animals and the unc-10(K77/79E) mutants exhibited synaptic depression following a 1 Hz or 5 Hz train stimulus.
source: Both the control animals and the unc-10(K77/79E) mutants exhibited synaptic depression following a 1 Hz or 5 Hz train stimulus (Figure 5A,C).
evidence: Demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings (Figure 5A,C).

claim: The unc-10(K77/79E) mutants displayed a similar depression rate to that of the control animals.
source: The unc-10(K77/79E) mutants displayed a similar depression rate to that of the control animals (Figure 5B,D), indicating that RIM binding to the C2A domain is not required for synaptic depression.
evidence: Shown by quantification of synaptic depression (Figure 5B,D).

claim: RIM binding to the C2A domain is not required for synaptic depression.
source: indicating that RIM binding to the C2A domain is not required for synaptic depression.
evidence: Inferred from similar depression rates in control and unc-10(K77/79E) mutants.

claim: No difference in the recovery rate was observed between the control animals and the unc-10(K77/79E) mutants.
source: As shown in Figure 5F, no difference in the recovery rate was observed between the control animals and the unc-10(K77/79E) mutants.
evidence: Demonstrated by paired-pulse recordings (Figure 5F).

claim: Disrupting C2A/RIM binding does not affect refilling of the SVs at synapses.
source: This indicates that disrupting C2A/RIM binding does not affect refilling of the SVs at synapses.
evidence: Inferred from normal recovery rates in unc-10(K77/79E) mutants.

claim: A truncated Munc13-1 lacking the N-terminal C2A domain is fully able to mediate vesicle priming in chromaffin cells.
source: In contrast, studies in chromaffin cells have shown that a truncated Munc13-1 lacking the N-terminal C2A domain is fully able to mediate vesicle priming (Betz et al., 2001)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work in chromaffin cells.

claim: Removing the N-terminal C2A domain from UNC-13L does not cause a change in the size of the RRP.
source: Similarly, a recent study in C. elegans found that removing the N-terminal C2A domain from UNC-13L, a Munc13-1 homolog, does not cause a change in the size of the RRP (Zhou et al., 2013a).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work in C. elegans.

claim: Munc13-1 is required for the docking and priming of synaptic vesicles.
source: Various studies have demonstrated that Munc13-1, a protein with multiple functional domains, is required for the docking and priming (Aravamudan et al., 1999; Augustin et al., 1999; Richmond et al., 1999)
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Munc13-1 is required for post-priming Ca2+-triggered SV release.
source: as well as post-priming Ca2+-triggered SV release (Basu et al., 2007; Chen et al., 2013; Hu et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The functions of Munc13-1 in docking, priming, and release are believed to be mediated by its central MUN domain.
source: The functions of Munc13-1 in these processes are believed to be mediated by its central MUN domain, which directly interacts with syntaxin and promotes SNARE assembly (Ma et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on the MUN domain.

claim: The C2A domain binds to the zinc finger (ZF) domain of RIM.
source: Betz et al. first found that the C2A domain binds to the zinc finger (ZF) domain of RIM, an active zone protein that is required for SV priming (Betz et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to the original discovery.

claim: A double mutation in rat RIM2α's ZF domain (K97/99E) disrupts C2A/RIM heterodimerization.
source: A double mutation in rat RIM2α's ZF domain (K97/99E) disrupts C2A/RIM heterodimerization (Dulubova et al., 2005)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The K97/99E mutation in RIM2α produces a large reduction in the readily releasable pool (RRP) of SVs.
source: and was subsequently shown to produce a large reduction in the readily releasable pool (RRP) of SVs (Deng et al., 2011; Camacho et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: C2A binding to RIM plays an important role in SV priming.
source: indicating that C2A binding to RIM plays an important role in SV priming.
evidence: Inferred from the reduction in RRP when C2A/RIM binding is disrupted, as reported in cited studies.

claim: The C2A domain forms a homodimer, thereby promoting formation of Munc13-1 homodimers.
source: Apart from forming a heterodimer with RIM, the C2A domain also forms a homodimer, thereby promoting formation of Munc13-1 homodimers (Lu et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Homodimerization of the C2A domain is not necessary for SV priming and post-priming SV release.
source: This homodimerization, however, is not necessary for SV priming and post-priming SV release (Camacho et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Deleting Munc13-1 C2A or disrupting C2A/RIM heterodimerization leads to a similar reduction in the size of the RRP to that observed in RIM knockout neurons.
source: In fact, deleting Munc13-1 C2A or disrupting C2A/RIM heterodimerization leads to a similar reduction in the size of the RRP to that observed in RIM knockout neurons (Deng et al., 2011; Camacho et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies in mouse neurons.

claim: The number of docked SVs is slightly decreased in the unc-10 mutant.
source: Electron microscopy results have revealed that the number of docked SVs is slightly decreased in the unc-10 mutant (Koushika et al., 2001; Weimer et al., 2006; Gracheva et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous electron microscopy studies.

claim: The slight decrease in docked SVs in unc-10 mutants cannot account for the far more dramatic SV fusion defect.
source: which cannot account for the far more dramatic SV fusion defect, suggesting a post-docking role of RIM in the active zone.
evidence: Inferred from the mismatch between the magnitude of docking and fusion defects.

claim: The size of the RRP in unc-10 mutants is comparable to that in the wild-type animals.
source: Consistent with these relatively minor docking defects, we found that the size of the RRP in unc-10 mutants (assessed by sucrose evoked currents) is comparable to that in the wild-type animals (data not shown)
evidence: Based on unpublished data from sucrose-evoked current measurements.

claim: UNC-10/RIM is not required for SV priming.
source: demonstrating that UNC-10/RIM is not required for SV priming.
evidence: Inferred from normal RRP size in unc-10 mutants.

claim: UNC-10/RIM primarily regulates SV fusion by increasing release probability and not by promoting SV priming.
source: These results suggest that UNC-10/RIM primarily regulates SV fusion by increasing release probability and not by promoting SV priming.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of normal priming but reduced release in unc-10 mutants.

claim: UNC-10/RIM increases release probability via its ability to bind UNC-13 and through its requirement for recruiting CaV2 calcium channels to presynaptic terminals.
source: UNC-10/RIM increases release probability via its ability to bind UNC-13 but also through its requirement for recruiting CaV2 calcium channels to presynaptic terminals (Han et al., 2011; Kaeser et al., 2011; Müller et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on RIM's multiple functions.

claim: SV priming is thought to consist of two sequential steps, termed molecular and positional priming.
source: SV priming is thought to consist of two sequential steps, termed molecular and positional priming (Neher and Sakaba, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous theoretical work.

claim: Molecular priming is proposed to account for a slow component of release, which consists of fusion of SVs that are docked far from calcium channels driving release.
source: Molecular priming is proposed to account for a slow component of release, which consists of fusion of SVs that are docked far from calcium channels driving release.
evidence: Based on established models of synaptic vesicle priming.

claim: Positional priming is proposed to mediate a faster form of release, which comprises fusion of SVs that are docked very close to calcium channels.
source: Positional priming is proposed to mediate a faster form of release, which comprises fusion of SVs that are docked very close to calcium channels.
evidence: Based on established models of synaptic vesicle priming.

claim: Worms may rely less on positional priming and instead rely more on molecular priming.
source: One possibility is that worms rely less on positional priming, which presumably requires UNC-13/RIM interaction, and instead rely more on molecular priming.
evidence: Speculative explanation for differences between worm and mouse phenotypes.

claim: Mice may require positional priming to maintain the RRP, and thus RIM mutants would have significant priming defects.
source: By contrast, mice may require positional priming to maintain the RRP, and thus RIM mutants would have significant priming defects.
evidence: Speculative explanation for differences between worm and mouse phenotypes.

claim: Tonic release has been proposed to have a different regulatory mechanism from evoked release.
source: This is confirmed by our observations in relation to tonic release, which has been proposed to have a different regulatory mechanism from evoked release (Ramirez and Kavalali, 2011; Melom et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A point mutation in the C1 domain of Munc13-1 accelerates hypertonicity-induced SV release without changing the size of the RRP.
source: Prior studies have shown that a point mutation in the C1 domain of Munc13-1 accelerates hypertonicity-induced SV release without changing the size of the RRP (Basu et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Transgenic C. elegans rescued by a truncated UNC-13L lacking its C1 or C2B domain exhibit a normal RRP.
source: Transgenic C. elegans rescued by a truncated UNC-13L lacking its C1 or C2B domain also exhibit a normal RRP (Michelassi et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Expression of a mutated Munc13-1 (P827L) leads to a significant increase in release probability without causing an increase in the size of the RRP.
source: Expression of a mutated Munc13-1 (P827L, located in the linker domain between C2B and MUN) leads to a significant increase in release probability without causing an increase in the size of the RRP (Lipstein et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The regulatory domains in UNC-13L (e.g. C2A, C1 and C2B) alter release probability but are not required for SV priming.
source: These observations appear to support the notion that the regulatory domains in UNC-13L (e.g. C2A, C1 and C2B) alter release probability but are not required for SV priming.
evidence: Inferred from multiple studies showing domain deletions affect release but not priming.

claim: UNC-13 has multiple regulatory effects on synaptic strength and plasticity, which are achieved by differential control of release probability by its various functional domains.
source: Thus, our results, together with the findings from other studies in C. elegans and mouse, suggest that UNC-13 has multiple regulatory effects on synaptic strength and plasticity, which are achieved by differential control of release probability by its various functional domains.
evidence: Inferred from the collective evidence of domain-specific effects on release probability.

claim: The Munc13 C2A domain has three binding states: homodimer, heterodimer, and monomer.
source: It has been proposed that the Munc13 C2A domain has three binding states, homodimer, heterodimer, and monomer, and that these three forms may co-exist in synaptic terminals.
evidence: Based on established models from previous research.

claim: Homodimerization of the C2A domain inhibits SV release.
source: Thus, our results support the notion that homodimerization of the C2A domain inhibits SV release
evidence: Inferred from rescue experiments showing restoration of release when homodimerization is blocked.

claim: RIM releases the C2A domain from the autoinhibitory homodimeric complex by competitively binding the C2A domain to form a heterodimer.
source: and that RIM releases the C2A domain from the autoinhibitory homodimeric complex by competitively binding the C2A domain to form a heterodimer, thereby allowing the C2A domain to become fusion-competent.
evidence: Inferred from the rescue of synaptic defects by blocking homodimerization in RIM mutants.

claim: The heterodimer itself does not produce an additional effect on synaptic transmission.
source: The heterodimer itself, however, does not produce an additional effect on synaptic transmission.
evidence: Inferred from the complete rescue by monomeric C2A in double mutants.

claim: All mApple-tagged UNC-13L constructs rescued the SV release in the unc-13 mutants, and the phenotypes were similar to those rescued by corresponding untagged UNC13L constructs.
source: All mApple-tagged UNC-13L constructs rescued the SV release in the unc-13 mutants, and the phenotypes were similar to those rescued by corresponding untagged UNC13L constructs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings comparing tagged and untagged constructs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

claim: C-terminal mCherry tags do not interfere with UNC-13's function in promoting SV exocytosis.
source: Our prior study showed that c-terminal mCherry tags do not interfere with UNC-13's function in promoting SV exocytosis (Hu et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.
